title: Intracellular polyamines regulate redox homeostasis with cAMP–PKA signalling during sexual mating/filamentation and pathogenicity of Sporisorium scitamineum

sections.abstract:
Sugarcane smut caused by Sporisorium scitamineum seriously impairs sugarcane production and quality. Sexual mating/filamentation is a critical step of S. scitamineum pathogenesis, yet the regulatory mechanisms are not fully understood. In this study, we identified the SsAGA , SsODC , and SsSAMDC genes, which are involved in polyamine biosynthesis in S. scitamineum . Deletion of SsODC led to complete loss of filamentous growth after sexual mating, and deletion of SsAGA or SsSAMDC caused reduced filamentation. Double deletion of SsODC and SsSAMDC resulted in auxotrophy for putrescine (PUT) and spermidine (SPD) when grown on minimal medium (MM), indicating that these two genes encode enzymes that are critical for PUT and SPD biosynthesis. We further showed that low PUT concentrations promoted S. scitamineum filamentation, while high PUT concentrations suppressed filamentation. Disrupted fungal polyamine biosynthesis also resulted in a loss of pathogenicity and reduced fungal biomass within infected plants at the early infection stage. SPD formed a gradient from the diseased part to nonsymptom parts of the cane stem, suggesting that SPD is probably favourable for fungal virulence. Mutants of the cAMP–PKA (SsGPA3–SsUAC1–SsADR1) signalling pathway displayed up‐regulation of the SsODC gene and elevated intracellular levels of PUT. SsODC directly interacted with SsGPA3, and sporidia of the ss1uac1 Δ odc Δ mutant displayed abundant pseudohyphae. Furthermore, we found that elevated PUT levels caused accumulation of intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS), probably by suppressing transcription of ROS‐scavenging enzymes, while SPD played the opposite role. Overall, our work proves that polyamines play important roles in the pathogenic development of sugarcane smut fungus, probably by collaboratively regulating intracellular redox homeostasis with the cAMP–PKA signalling pathway.

Keywords: cAMP–PKA signalling pathway, pathogenesis, polyamines, redox, sexual mating/filamentation, Sporisorium scitamineum
sections.introduction:
Sugarcane smut is one of the main fungal diseases that seriously reduce sugarcane production. The causal pathogen, Sporisorium scitamineum , is a typical dimorphic fungus. Its life cycle has three stages, namely, the haploid sporidium stage, the dikaryotic hypha stage, and the diploid teliospore stage (Piepenbring et al., 2002 ). Haploid yeast‐type sporidia are unable to infect the host and are of two opposite mating types, MAT‐1 and MAT‐2 . Dikaryotic hyphae are formed after sexual mating of haploid sporidia of different mating types, and are capable of infecting host canes (Yan, Zhu, et al., 2016 ). After sexual mating, the b locus encoding a heterodimeric transcription factor complex consisting of bE and bW proteins from different alleles controls filamentous growth in S. scitamineum (Yan, Zhu, et al., 2016 ). The dikaryotic hyphae grow within the sugarcane stem and form teliospores wrapped by plant tissue and as a “whip” shape, the typical symptom of sugarcane smut disease. Therefore, understanding the regulatory mechanism underlying sexual mating/filamentation and teliospore formation of S. scitamineum is critical for the development of efficient disease management strategies.

Two classical signalling pathways, the mitogen‐activated protein kinase (MAPK) and cAMP/protein kinase A (PKA) pathways, regulate the sexual mating process in smut fungi (Chang et al., 2019 ; Deng et al., 2018 ; Kaffarnik et al., 2003 ; Muller et al., 1999 , 2003 ). In Ustilago maydis , the MAPK and cAMP–PKA pathways coordinate to regulate sexual mating and the yeast‐to‐hypha dimorphic transition (Lengeler et al., 2000 ). The core elements of the cAMP–PKA pathway include the G‐protein GPA3, the adenylyl cyclase UAC1, and the cAMP‐dependent PKA ADR1 (Lee et al., 2003 ; Leveleki et al., 2004 ). Pheromones could be perceived by pheromone receptors and/or GPCR, and the signal transduction depends on the GPA3–UAC1–ADR1 (cAMP–PKA) signalling pathway and the Kpp4–Fuz7–Kpp2 (MAPK) signalling cascade, with partial overlap, commonly inducing the a locus, which encodes the pheromone precursors Mfa1/2 and receptors Pra1/2, through the transcription factor Prf1 (Kaffarnik et al., 2003 ; Muller et al., 1999 , 2003 ; Zhu et al., 2019 ), to trigger mating, filamentation, and virulence.

Polyamines, which are biologically active aliphatic nitrogen‐containing bases, are ubiquitously present in living organisms and have important biological functions as signalling molecules (Rocha & Wilson, 2019 ). According to the number of amino groups in the chemical structure, amines are divided into monoamines, including putrescine (PUT) and cadaverine (CAD); triamines, including spermidine (SPD); and tetramines, including spermine (SPM). Many fungal species do not produce SPM. PUT, SPD, and SPM are important for cell growth, and their biosynthesis pathways differ among plants, bacteria, animals, and fungi (Miller‐Fleming et al., 2015 ; Valdes‐Santiago, Cervantes‐Chavez, Leon‐Ramirez et al., 2012 ). So far, two pathways for PUT biosynthesis have been reported, in which l ‐arginine is either hydrolysed by arginase (AGA) to generate ornithine, which is then decarboxylated by ornithine decarboxylase (ODC) to produce PUT, or catalysed sequentially by arginine decarboxylase (ADC), agmatinase (AGT), and agmatine iminohydrolase (AIH) to produce PUT. Meanwhile, S ‐adenosyl methionine (SAM) is decarboxylated by SAM decarboxylase (SAMDC) to generate decarboxylated SAM (dcSAM), which is a critical substrate for the synthesis of SPD and SPM from the upstream metabolites, PUT and SPD, respectively; these reactions are catalysed by SPD synthase (SPDS) and SPM synthase (SPMS), respectively (Shah & Swiatlo, 2008 ; Valdes‐Santiago, Cervantes‐Chavez, Leon‐Ramirez, et al., 2012 ; Valdes‐Santiago & Ruiz‐Herrera, 2013 ). At present, little is known about polyamine biosynthesis and their mechanism of action in fungi, including S. scitamineum .

In the present study, we identified the polyamine biosynthesis genes SsAGA , SsODC , and SsSAMDC in S. scitamineum and characterized their functions by reverse genetics. Our study provides evidence that polyamine homeostasis is important for sexual mating/filamentation in S. scitamineum . Low concentrations of PUT promoted and high concentrations of PUT suppressed filamentous growth after sexual mating in S. scitamineum . SPD promoted filamentation at a wide range of concentrations. The polyamine synthesis pathway genetically and physically interacted with the cAMP–PKA signalling pathway to regulate sexual mating/filamentation and mediate the S. scitamineum –sugarcane interaction, probably by modulating intracellular redox homeostasis. Overall, our work reveals the roles of polyamines in regulating growth and pathogenic development of S. scitamineum and the underlying mechanism, thus providing a theoretical basis for designing prevention and control strategies of sugarcane smut disease.
sections.results:
In order to elucidate the polyamine biosynthesis pathway in S. scitamineum , we used the key enzymes of the polyamine biosynthesis pathway reported in U. maydis as the queries to perform a BLASTP search ( https://blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/Blast.cgi?PROGRAM=blastp&PAGE_TYPE=BlastSearch&LINK_LOC=blasthome ). As shown in Table 1 , a putative arginase ( CDU25136.1 , named SsAGA), an ornithine decarboxylase ( CDU24605.1 , named SsODC), and a SAM decarboxylase ( CDU24548.1 , named SsSAMDC) were identified based on amino acid sequence similarity. We performed phylogenetic analysis using these proteins and their orthologues from smut fungi or ascomycetes (Table S1 ). The results showed that SsAGA, SsODC, and SsSAMDC were conserved in a diverse range of fungal species, closest to the orthologues in Sporisorium reilianum , forming a clade with the orthologues from smut fungi and separate from the clade formed by ascomycetous orthologues (Figure S1 ).

Identification of genes involved in polyamine biosynthesis.

By homologous recombination we generated deletion mutants of SsAGA , SsODC , and SsSAMDC in both MAT‐1 and MAT‐2 backgrounds, as verified by Southern blotting (Figure S2a–c ). We named the single‐deletion mutants ss1aga Δ and ss2aga Δ, ss1odc Δ and ss2odc Δ, and ss1samdc Δ and ss2samdc Δ, respectively. The genetic complementation strains for ss1odc Δ, ss2odc Δ, ss1samdc Δ, and ss2samdc Δ were generated, namely, Ss1ODC‐COM , Ss2ODC‐COM , Ss1SAMDC‐COM , and Ss2SAMDC‐COM , and verified by PCR (Figure S2b,c ) or fluorescence microscopic observation of the fused SsODC‐mCherry and SsSAMDC‐mCherry proteins (Figure S3b ). We also generated an ss2odc Δ samdc Δ double mutant (Figure S2d ). For all the deletion mutants and complementation strains, at least two independent strains were obtained and used for the characterization of polyamine biosynthesis and the biological functions. The results are described below.

We found that loss of SsSAMDC led to an obvious defect in sporidial growth on minimal medium (MM), which could be restored by supplementation with SPD (1 mM; Figure 1a ). This indicates that SsSAMDC is critical for SPD biosynthesis, probably using PUT as a substrate. Sporidial growth of the ss2aga Δ and ss2odc Δ mutants was comparable to that of the wild‐type (WT) MAT‐2 strain (Figure 1a ). Furthermore, we found that the double mutant ss2odc Δ samdc Δ was auxotrophic when grown on MM in low‐inoculum cultures (10 3 –10 6 cells), which could be restored by supplementation with PUT or SPD (both 1 mM; Figure 1b ). Interestingly, such auxotrophy of the ss2odc Δ samdc Δ double mutant was not obvious when sporidia were grown on yeast extract‐peptone‐sucrose medium (YePS) or potato dextrose agar (PDA) (Figure 1b ). We infer that YePS or PDA contained PUT and/or SPD, which could be utilized by ss2odc Δ samdc Δ, thus masking its PUT or SPD auxotrophy.

Assessment of the roles of SsAGA, SsODC, and SsSAMDC in polyamine biosynthesis in Sporisorium scitamineum . (a, b) Haploid growth of wild‐type ( MAT‐2 ) and mutant strains on solid minimal medium (MM). Fresh haploid sporidia were cultured in liquid yeast extract‐peptone‐sucrose (YePS) medium, washed twice with double‐distilled water, and adjusted to OD 600 = 1.0, before serial dilution (OD 600 = 1.0, 0.1, 0.01, 0.001, 0.0001) and spotting onto solid MM. Putrescine (PUT), spermidine (SPD), or spermine (SPM) was added to MM to a final concentration of 1 mM, and MM served as a control. Images were taken after 2–3 days of cultivation. (c) The mass spectra of polyamines detected in MAT‐2 and ss2odc Δ samdc Δ sporidia. Black line, PUT; red line, SPD; RT, retention time. (d) Quantification of intracellular polyamines of MAT‐2 and ss2odc Δ samdc Δ. Fresh haploid sporidia were cultured in liquid YePS medium for 12 h, washed twice with double‐distilled water, and adjusted to OD 600 = 1.0. Polyamine contents were measured by liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry using crude extracts of fungal cells. Bar chart depicts the mean ± SE derived from three independent biological repeats, each with three replicates ( n = 3). * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01.

Given that the ss2odc Δ samdc Δ double mutant was auxotrophic for PUT and SPD, we assessed the roles of SsODC and SsSAMDC in S. scitamineum polyamine biosynthesis by liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (LC‐MS) analysis. As WT or mutant sporidia could not grow in liquid MM, we cultured the sporidia in liquid YePS medium, to reach 10 7 cells for polyamine extraction. Serially diluted PUT (0.004, 0.01, 0.02, 0.03, 0.05 mM) and SPD (0.004, 0.01, 0.02, 0.03, 0.05 mM) standards were detected as peaks with m / z ratios of 297.16 and 458.24, respectively. A peak with a retention time (RT) of 2.60 min corresponds to PUT, and a peak with an RT of 4.50 min corresponds to SPD (Figure 1c ). Indeed, PUT and SPD could be detected in YePS medium (Figure 1c ). Subsequently, we compared the intracellular levels of PUT and SPD in ss2odc Δ samdc Δ sporidia to those in MAT‐2 sporidia. The result showed that the PUT content in ss2odc Δ samdc Δ was as low as 12.73% of that in MAT‐2 , and the SPD content in ss2odc Δ samdc Δ was about 10.67% of that in MAT‐2 (Figure 1d ).

Overall, these results confirm that SsSAMDC is critical for SPD biosynthesis, and both SsODC and SsSAMDC are likely to contribute to PUT biosynthesis.

To determine the role of polyamines in S. scitamineum mating/filamentation, dikaryotic hyphal growth after asexual mating was assessed in the mutants. The results showed that ss1odc Δ × ss2odc Δ had almost no dikaryotic hyphae at all, and filamentation of ss1aga Δ × ss2aga Δ, ss1samdc Δ × ss2samdc Δ, or MAT‐1 × ss2odc Δ samdc Δ was reduced compared to MAT‐1 × MAT‐2 when grown on PDA (Figure 2a ). When cultured on MM, neither WT MAT‐1 × MAT‐2 nor MAT‐1 × ss2odc Δ samdc Δ was able to mate and form dikaryotic hyphae at all (Figure S3a ).

Polyamine biosynthesis genes are involved in Sporisorium scitamineum sexual mating/filamentation. (a) Mating assay of wild‐type (WT; MAT‐1 × MAT‐2 ) and polyamine mutants ( ssaga Δ, ss1aga Δ × ss2aga Δ; ssodc Δ, ss1odc Δ × ss2odc Δ; sssamdc Δ, ss1samdc Δ × ss2samdc Δ; ΔΔ, MAT‐1 × ss2odc Δ samdc Δ). Fresh haploid sporidia were cultured in liquid yeast extract‐peptone‐sucrose (YePS) medium for 12 h, washed twice with double‐distilled water, and adjusted to OD 600 = 1.0. Equal volumes of compatible wild‐type or mutant sporidia of opposite mating types were mixed and spotted onto potato dextrose agar (PDA) with or without 100 mM putrescine (PUT), 1000 mM spermidine (SPD), or 100 mM spermine (SPM). The mating cultures were incubated at 28°C for 2–3 days, followed by observation and imaging. Scale bar = 1 mm. (b) Mating assay of wild‐type (WT; MAT‐1 × MAT‐2 ) under control conditions or with PUT, SPD, or SPM at various concentrations. Inocula were 10 4 /mL. Scale bar = 1 mm. (c) Transcriptional profiles of sexual mating genes in ss1aga Δ × ss2aga Δ, ss1odc Δ × ss2odc Δ, and ss1samdc Δ × ss2samdc Δ mutants, in comparison to MAT‐1 × MAT‐2 . The relative gene expression levels were calculated according to the 2 −ΔΔ C t method (Livak & Schmittgen, 2001 ), with Actin as an internal control. Bar chart depicts the mean ± SE derived from three independent biological repeats, each with three replicates ( n = 3). * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001, **** p < 0.0001; ns indicates no statistical significance.

To further verify the roles of polyamines in S. scitamineum sexual mating/filamentation, we first determined the dose‐dependent effect of PUT, SPD, or SPM on WT MAT‐1 × MAT‐2 grown on PDA. The results showed that PUT at 10–100 mM could slightly promote filamentation, while high concentrations of PUT suppressed filamentation (Figure 2b ). SPD at 10–1000 mM and SPM at 10–100 mM could also promote filamentation (Figure 2b ). Next, we supplied 100 mM PUT, 1000 mM SPD, or 100 mM SPM to the mating cultures of ss1aga Δ × ss2aga Δ, ss1odc Δ × ss2odc Δ, ss1samdc Δ × ss2samdc Δ, and MAT‐1 × ss2odc Δ samdc Δ. The results showed that 1,000 mM SPD or 100 mM SPM could slightly restore filamentation of ss1aga Δ × ss2aga Δ, ss1samdc Δ × ss2samdc Δ, and MAT‐1 × ss2odc Δ samdc Δ. Similarly, exogenous supplementation of SPD (1000 mM) or SPM (100 mM) could slightly induce hyphal growth for MAT‐1 × ss2odc Δ samdc Δ grown on MM (Figure S3a ).

Sexual mating/filamentation could be restored in the complementation strains Ss1ODC‐COM × Ss2ODC‐COM and Ss1SAMDC‐COM × Ss2SAMDC‐COM to a comparable level as WT (Figure S3b ), confirming that the SsODC and SsSAMDC genes are indeed required for S. scitamineum sexual mating/filamentation. Reverse transcription‐quantitative PCR (RT‐qPCR) analysis was performed in mutants versus WT to evaluate the relative expression levels of the genes known to be involved in sexual mating/filamentation, including SsGPA3 , SsUAC1 , SsKPP2 , SsbE , SsbW , and SsPRF1 . We noticed that the relative expression level of SsUAC1 was down‐regulated in ss1odc Δ × ss2odc Δ, while SsbW and SsPRF1 were down‐regulated in ss1samdc Δ × ss2samdc Δ (Figure 2c ).

Overall, our results showed that the SsAGA , SsODC , and SsSAMDC genes are all important for sexual mating/filamentation of S. scitamineum , probably by contributing to polyamine biosynthesis.

We further assessed the roles of polyamine biosynthesis pathway genes in S. scitamineum virulence. We inoculated the seedlings of a susceptible sugarcane cultivar (ROC22) with 1 mL of a mixture (1:1, vol/vol) of MAT‐1 × MAT‐2 , ss1aga Δ × ss2aga Δ, ss1odc Δ × ss2odc Δ, or ss1samdc Δ × ss2samdc Δ. Disease symptoms were visible at 3–6 months post‐infection, only in the seedlings infected by WT MAT‐1 × MAT‐2 (Figure 3a ), with an incidence rate of 37.5% ± 2.5%. In contrast, no black whip symptom was found in the seedlings infected by ss1aga Δ × ss2aga Δ, ss1odc Δ × ss2odc Δ, or ss1samdc Δ × ss2samdc Δ or in blank controls inoculated with double‐distilled water (ddH 2 O) (Figure 3a ). We further measured the average plant height as an indicator of smut fungus infection and found that the mutant‐infected plants or noninfected plants were significantly taller than the WT MAT‐1 × MAT‐2 ‐infected seedlings (Figure 3b ).

Spermidine (SPD) is required for virulence of Sporisorium scitamineum . (a) Pathogenicity assay. Mixed sporidia (1 mL) of MAT‐1 × MAT‐2 , ss1aga Δ × ss2aga Δ, ss1odc Δ × ss2odc Δ, and ss1samdc Δ × ss2samdc Δ were injected into the seedlings of sugarcane cultivar ROC22, with double‐distilled water (ddH 2 O) serving as a blank control. Each treatment contained at least 15 seedlings ( n = 15). The red boxed region is enlarged, showing the “black whip” symptoms appearing on top of seedlings infected by WT ( MAT‐1 × MAT‐2 ). (b) Quantitative analysis of the height of infected seedlings versus wild type (WT). n = 17, 10, 10, 12, and 15, respectively. (c) Quantitative analysis of fungal biomass by quantitative PCR. Mixed sporidia of MAT‐1 × MAT‐2 , ss1aga Δ × ss2aga Δ, ss1odc Δ × ss2odc Δ, or ss1samdc Δ × ss2samdc Δ were injected into sugarcane seedlings, and the infected stems (about 3 cm) were sampled for DNA extraction at 3 and 7 days post‐inoculation (dpi). The relative biomass level was calculated according to the 2 −ΔΔ C t method, using the fungal Actin gene and the sugarcane GAPDH gene as internal controls. Bar chart depicts the mean ± SE derived from three independent biological repeats, each with three replicates ( n = 3). (d) Transcriptional profile of S. scitamineum polyamine metabolism genes during the early stage of sugarcane infection (0, 3, and 7 dpi). Approximately 3‐cm stems of the inoculated site were sampled for RNA extraction. The relative gene expression levels were calculated according to the 2 −ΔΔ C t method (Livak & Schmittgen, 2001 ), with Actin as an internal control. Bar chart depicts the mean ± SE derived from three independent biological repeats, each with three replicates ( n = 3). (e) Polyamine levels in the top (diseased tissue, “whip”), middle, or bottom parts of stems of the sugarcane seedlings infected by wild type (WT; MAT‐1 × MAT‐2 ). Uninfected, healthy sugarcane seedlings were used as a control. The sampled stems (1 g) were ground in liquid nitrogen, and the crude extracts were analysed by liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry to determine the polyamine contents. PUT, putrescine. Bar chart depicts the mean ± SE derived from three independent biological repeats, each with three replicates ( n = 3). For (b), (c), (d), and (e), * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001, **** p < 0.0001; ns indicates no statistical significance.

To explore the possible role of polyamine biosynthesis in the early stage of S. scitamineum infection, we measured the fungal biomass in the infected seedlings by qPCR at 3 and 7 days post‐infection (dpi). The results showed that the biomass of mutants at 3 dpi was comparable to that of WT MAT‐1 × MAT‐2 , while at 7 dpi the biomass of ss1odc Δ × ss2odc Δ and ss1samdc Δ × ss2samdc Δ was much lower than that of WT (Figure 3c ).

To investigate the functional mechanism of fungus‐derived polyamines during host infection, we quantitatively assessed the expression levels of polyamine metabolism genes at 0, 3, and 7 dpi. The results showed that SsSAMDC and SsSPDS / SPMS ( SPSC_01548 ) were up‐regulated 1.81‐fold and 1.57‐fold at 3 dpi and 1.79‐fold and 1.91‐fold at 7 dpi, respectively (Figure 3d ). In contrast, SsAGA and SsPAO ( SPSC_01582 ) were down‐regulated to 0.50‐fold and 0.46‐fold at 3 dpi and to 0.14‐fold and 0.28‐fold at 7 dpi, respectively (Figure 3d ). The transcriptional profiles suggest that at the early stage of infection, S. scitamineum tends to down‐regulate genes for PUT biosynthesis but up‐regulate genes for SPD biosynthesis.

We also measured polyamine levels in diseased tissue—the “whip” form at the top of cane stems—and compared these to those in the middle and bottom parts of the stems of the infected sugarcane seedlings. Uninfected, healthy sugarcane seedlings served as a control. The results showed that PUT and SPD contents were significantly higher in the infected sugarcane stems than in healthy sugarcane stems (Figure 3e ). In addition, SPD content displayed a gradient from the top (“whip”) to the bottom of infected sugarcane, while SPD was not present in healthy sugarcane (Figure 3e ). The results indicated that SPD accumulates in the top stems of infected sugarcane, where the dikaryotic hyphae grow towards, and the whip symptoms develop as disease progresses. Therefore, we infer that S. scitamineum may induce SsSAMDC and SsSPDS / SPMS expression in the early stage of infection, probably to generate SPD to facilitate infection and promote virulence.

Overall, we conclude that disruption of the polyamine biosynthesis pathway results in reduced or loss of pathogenicity/virulence of S. scitamineum .

It has previously been reported that the cAMP–PKA signalling pathway, which is composed of SsGPA3, SsUAC1, and SsADR1, controls sexual mating/filamentation in S. scitamineum (Chang et al., 2019 ). To investigate the relationship (if any) between polyamines and the cAMP–PKA signalling pathway, we exogenously added polyamines to MAT‐1 (WT), ss1gpa3 Δ, ss1uac1 Δ, ss1adr1 Δ, and ss1prf1 Δ and observed the effect on sexual mating/filamentation. SPM (100 μM) slightly increased sexual mating/filamentation of WT, ss1gpa3 Δ, ss1uac1 Δ, and ss1adr1 Δ. Meanwhile, SPD (1 mM) could effectively restore sexual mating/filamentation of ss1gpa3 Δ, ss1uac1 Δ, and ss1adr1 Δ (Figure 4a ). Dikaryotic hyphal growth was completely blocked in ss1prf1 Δ (Figure 4a ) and could not be restored by exogenous addition of polyamines.

The cAMP–PKA signalling pathway regulates polyamine metabolism. (a) Mating assay of wild type (WT; MAT‐1 × MAT‐2 ) and cAMP–PKA mutants ( ssgpa3 Δ, ss1gpa3 Δ × MAT‐2 ; ssuac1 Δ, ss1uac1 Δ × MAT‐2 ; ssadr1 Δ, ss1adr1 Δ × MAT‐2 ; ssprf1 Δ, ss1prf1 Δ × MAT‐2 ). Mixed WT or mutant haploid sporidia (OD 600 = 1.0) were spotted onto potato dextrose agar (PDA) with or without 100 μM putrescine (PUT), 1000 μM spermidine (SPD), or 100 μM spermine (SPM). The mating cultures were incubated at 28°C for 2–3 days, followed by observation and imaging. Scale bar = 1 mm. (b) Transcriptional profile of polyamine biosynthesis pathway genes in the cAMP–PKA mutants in comparison to MAT‐1 . Bar chart depicts the mean ± SE derived from three independent biological repeats, each with three replicates ( n = 3). (c) Measurement of intracellular polyamines of MAT‐1 , ss1gpa3 Δ, ss1uac1 Δ, ss1adr1 Δ, and ss1prf1 Δ. Bar chart depicts the mean ± SE derived from three independent biological repeats, each with three replicates ( n = 3). For (b) and (c), * p < 0.05, **** p < 0.0001; ns indicates no statistical significance. (d) Mating assay of WT ( MAT‐1 × MAT‐2 ) and polyamine mutants ( ssaga Δ, ss1aga Δ × ss2aga Δ; ssodc Δ, ss1odc Δ × ss2odc Δ; sssamdc Δ, ss1samdc Δ × ss2samdc Δ) with cAMP (1 or 10 mM) or under control conditions (PDA). Scale bar = 1 mm.

We analysed the relative expression levels of polyamine metabolism‐related genes in MAT‐1 , ss1gpa3 Δ, ss1uac1 Δ, ss1adr1 Δ, and ss1prf1 Δ by RT‐qPCR. SsODC was up‐regulated 6.48‐, 1.80‐, and 8.44‐fold in ss1gpa3 Δ, ss1uac1 Δ, and ss1adr1 Δ, respectively (Figure 4b ). Correspondingly, the PUT content was significantly higher in ss1gpa3 Δ, ss1uac1 Δ, ss1adr1 Δ, and ss1prf1 Δ than in MAT‐1 , while SPD or SPM levels were comparable to WT (Figure 4c ).

On the other hand, we noticed that cAMP at high concentrations inhibited sexual mating/filamentation of MAT‐1 × MAT‐2 and could not restore the sexual mating/filamentation of polyamine mutants (Figure 4d ). In addition, cAMP could effectively restore sexual mating/filamentation of ss1gpa3 Δ and ss1uac1 Δ but not ss1adr1 Δ (Figure S3c ), consistent with a previous report (Chang et al., 2019 ). Therefore, the cAMP–PKA signalling pathway may act upstream of polyamine biosynthesis.

To evaluate the physical interaction between polyamine biosynthesis and the cAMP–PKA signalling pathway, we carried out yeast two‐hybrid (Y2H) analysis. The results showed that SsODC directly interacted with SsGPA3 (Figure 5a ), but not with SsUAC1 or SsADR1 (Figure 5b ). In addition, SsODC formed a homodimer (Figure S3d ), consistent with a previous report (Wu et al., 2015 , 2022 ). Next, we generated ss1uac1 Δ odc Δ double‐deletion mutants by deleting SsODC in the ss1uac1 Δ background (Figure S2e ). Strikingly, ss1uac1 Δ odc Δ sporidia showed a filamentous phenotype under control conditions (Figure 5c ), and the sporidia showed a short, coarse, and irregular elliptic shape under the microscope, which was obviously different from that of MAT‐1 , ss1uac1 Δ, or ss1odc Δ (Figure 5d ). High‐concentration cAMP (10 mM) inhibited the filamentous phenotype of ss1uac1 Δ odc Δ without changing sporidial morphology (Figure 5c,d ), which is similar to the previously reported U. maydis uac1 mutant, which has a constitutively filamentous phenotype that could be restored by exogenous cAMP (Gold et al., 1994 ).

The polyamine biosynthesis pathway interacts with the cAMP–PKA signalling pathway. (a) Direct interaction between SsGPA3 and SsODC verified by yeast two‐hybrid (Y2H) analysis. SsGPA3 ‐pGADT7 and SsODC ‐pGBKT7 constructs were cointroduced into the yeast Y2H Gold strain (CAT#: YC1002S). The transformants were serially diluted and spotted on synthetic defined medium (SD)−Leu−Trp or SD−Ade−Leu−Trp−His medium and cultured for 3 days. The pair of plasmids pGADT7‐T and pGBKT7‐p53 was used as the positive control, and the pair of plasmids pGADT7 and pGBKT7 was used as the negative control. AD, the pGADT7 plasmid; BD, the pGBKT7 plasmid. (b) Y2H assay to investigate the interaction between SsUAC1 or SsADR1 and SsODC, following the same method as in (a). (c) Sporidial morphology of wild‐type ( MAT‐1 ), ss1uac1 Δ, ss1odc Δ, and ss1uac1 Δ odc Δ cultured on PDA with or without 10 mM cAMP or polyamines (1 mM PUT, 1 mM SPD, 0.1 mM SPM, 1 mM SPM). The sporidial cultures were incubated at 28°C for 2–3 days, followed by observation and imaging. Scale bar = 1 mm. (d) Microscopic observation of sporidial morphology of wild type ( MAT‐1 ), ss1uac1 Δ, ss1odc Δ, and ss1uac1 Δ odc Δ under control conditions or with cAMP. Scale bar = 10 μm.

Overall, our results demonstrate a direct interaction between SsGPA3 of the cAMP–PKA signalling pathway and SsODC of the polyamine biosynthesis pathway, suggesting a cross‐talk between the intracellular levels of polyamines and cAMP signalling to regulate S. scitamineum sexual mating/filamentation.

In order to elucidate the mechanisms underlying the regulatory effects of polyamines on sexual mating/filamentation, we performed comparative transcriptome analysis using WT MAT‐1 , ss1samdc Δ, and ss1aga Δ. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) (false discovery rate [FDR] < 0.05 and log 2 (fold change [FC]) > |1||; three biological repeats) were identified in the ss1samdc Δ mutant compared to the WT MAT‐1 strain and in ss1samdc Δ × ss2samdc Δ compared to MAT‐1 × MAT‐2 . The SsSAMDC‐encoding gene SPSC_04049 was among the significantly down‐regulated genes (log 2 [FC] = −9.23, FDR = 2.22 × 10 −67 ; log 2 [FC] = −9.18, FDR = 1.37 × 10 −129 , respectively; Dataset S1 ), indicating that the RNA sequencing (RNA‐seq) and transcriptome analysis data were reliable. For ss1samdc Δ versus MAT‐1 , a total of 726 DEGs were identified (Dataset S1 ). Gene Ontology (GO) and KEGG enrichment analyses indicated that various metabolic processes, such as biosynthesis of secondary metabolites like ferrichrome A, biosynthesis of amino acids, and autophagy, were potentially subject to regulation by SsSAMDC/SPD (Figure S4a,b ). For ss1samdc Δ × ss2samdc Δ versus MAT‐1 × MAT‐2 , a total of 875 DEGs were identified (Dataset S1 ), which were enriched in various metabolic processes such as fatty acid degradation and fatty acid metabolism (Figure S4c,d ). We found 291 DEGs that were common between ss1samdc Δ versus MAT‐1 and ss1samdc Δ × ss2samdc Δ versus MAT‐1 × MAT‐2 , 86 of which were up‐regulated and 205 were down‐regulated (Dataset S1 ).

In the same way, we obtained DEGs between ss1aga Δ versus MAT‐1 and ss1aga Δ × ss2aga Δ versus MAT‐1 × MAT‐2 . The SsAGA‐encoding gene SPSC_04970 was among the significantly down‐regulated genes (log 2 [FC] = −8.21, FDR = 4.37 × 10 −58 ; log 2 [FC] = −12.07, FDR = 4.65 × 10 −28 , respectively; Dataset S2 ), verifying that the RNA‐seq and transcriptome analysis data were reliable. For ss1aga Δ versus MAT‐1 , a total of 1112 DEGs were identified (Dataset S2 ). GO and KEGG enrichment analyses indicated that various metabolic processes, such as carbohydrate metabolism, amino acid metabolism, and lipid metabolism, were potentially subject to regulation by SsAGA (Figure S5a,b ). For ss1aga Δ × ss2aga Δ versus MAT‐1 × MAT‐2 , a total of 991 DEGs were identified (Dataset S2 ), which were enriched in various metabolic processes such as fatty acid degradation, fatty acid metabolism, and biosynthesis of secondary metabolites (Figure S5c,d ). We found 451 DEGs that were common between ss1aga Δ versus MAT‐1 and ss1aga Δ × ss2aga Δ versus MAT‐1 × MAT‐2 , 226 of which were up‐regulated and 225 were down‐regulated (Dataset S2 ). RT‐qPCR was performed to assess the expression levels of randomly selected genes in mutant strains in comparison to WT, and the results (Table S2 ) validated the comparative transcriptome analysis.

It was particularly interesting to notice that genes encoding antioxidant enzymes and/or reactive oxygen species (ROS) scavengers were significantly down‐regulated in ss1aga Δ sporidia as compared to WT (Dataset S2 ), suggesting that disrupted polyamine biosynthesis may lead to changes in redox homeostasis. Indeed, measurement of intracellular hydrogen peroxide (H 2 O 2 ) levels showed that the ss1aga Δ and ss1odc Δ mutants had elevated H 2 O 2 levels, while ss1samdc Δ showed no difference in H 2 O 2 levels compared to the WT MAT‐1 and MAT‐2 strains (Figure 6a ). The ss1uac1 Δ mutant showed a slight but insignificant decrease in H 2 O 2 levels ( p > 0.05), consistent with a previous report (Chang et al., 2019 ). Double deletion of SsUAC1 and SsODC led to increased H 2 O 2 levels, similar to the ss1odc Δ mutant (Figure 6a ).

Polyamines regulate redox homeostasis in Sporisorium scitamineum . (a) Measurement of intracellular H 2 O 2 levels of MAT‐1 , MAT‐2 , ss1aga Δ, ss1odc Δ, ss1samdc Δ, ss1uac1 Δ, and ss1uac1 Δ odc Δ. Fresh haploid sporidia were cultured on solid yeast extract‐peptone‐sucrose (YePS) medium for 2 days. H 2 O 2 levels were measured from crude extracts by the Amplex Red Hydrogen Peroxide/Peroxidase Assay Kit (ThermoFisher). Bar chart depicts the mean ± SE derived from three independent biological repeats, each with three replicates ( n = 3). (b) Evaluation of oxidative stress tolerance of wild type ( MAT‐2 ) and polyamine mutants grown on potato dextrose agar (PDA). Fresh haploid sporidia were cultured in liquid YePS medium, washed twice with double‐distilled water, and adjusted to OD 600 = 1.0, before serial dilution (OD 600 = 1.0, 0.1, 0.01, 0.001, 0.0001) and spotting onto PDA. H 2 O 2 was added to PDA to a final concentration of 0.5 or 1 mM, and PDA served as a control. Images were taken after 2–3 days of cultivation. (c) Transcriptional profile of reactive oxygen species (ROS) marker genes in MAT‐1 under H 2 O 2 treatment in combination with putrescine (PUT; 1 mM) or spermidine (SPD; 1 mM). Bar chart depicts the mean ± SE derived from three independent biological repeats, each with three replicates ( n = 3). CAT1, catalase; CAT2, catalase 2; GST, glutathione S ‐transferase; POD, peroxidase; PRX1, peroxiredoxin 1; SOD2, superoxide dismutase 2. For (a) and (c), * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001, **** p < 0.0001; ns indicates no statistical significance. (d) A proposed working model depicting the interactions between the polyamine biosynthesis pathway and the cAMP–PKA signalling pathway modulating intracellular redox homeostasis to regulate sexual mating/filamentation and pathogenicity of Sporisorium scitamineum . The image was created by Biorender.

We then evaluated tolerance to oxidative stress (0.5 or 1 mM H 2 O 2 ) of the mutants in comparison to the WT. The results showed that these mutants were more sensitive to H 2 O 2 compared to the WT ( MAT‐2 ; Figure 6b ). We assessed the transcript levels of genes involved in redox homeostasis and/or the response to oxidative stress in WT sporidia by RT‐qPCR. The results showed that PUT suppressed the transcription of antioxidant enzyme genes, including CAT1 , CAT2 , PRX1 , POD , and SOD2 (Figure 6c ). In contrast, SPD treatment led to up‐regulation of these enzymes under oxidative stress conditions (H 2 O 2 treatment; Figure 6c ). Overall, these results indicate that PUT suppresses S. scitamineum filamentation probably by increasing intracellular ROS levels, while SPD could decrease intracellular ROS levels by affecting the transcript levels of antioxidant enzyme genes.

In summary, our study demonstrates that SPD acts as a positive regulator of S. scitamineum sexual mating/filamentation and mediates the S. scitamineum –sugarcane interaction, probably to guide in planta growth of the infecting dikaryotic hyphae. PUT at low concentrations promoted filamentation, probably by acting as a substrate for SPD biosynthesis, while high concentrations of PUT suppressed sexual mating/filamentation, probably by promoting ROS accumulation and causing oxidative stress in the fungal cells. The polyamine biosynthesis pathway interacts with the cAMP–PKA signalling pathway to modulate intracellular redox homeostasis, which is important for S. scitamineum sexual mating/filamentation and pathogenesis. A working model is proposed as shown in Figure 6d .
sections.discussion:
Polyamines are aliphatic nitrogen‐containing bases that are widely present in organisms, having biological functions in important processes including cell growth, proliferation, development, and differentiation (Kusano et al., 2008 ; Michael, 2016 ; Miller‐Fleming et al., 2015 ). Polyamines are reported to regulate ion channel function (Williams, 1997 ), nucleic acid packaging, DNA replication, apoptosis, gene transcription, and translation (Ruan et al., 1994 ). Polyamines maintain nucleic acid stability and regulate protein synthesis by acting as electrostatic bridges between the phosphate charges of DNA/RNA and various other highly charged linear chains, such as actin filaments and microtubules (Tang et al., 1996 ), using their multivalent cations. Plants utilize polyamines to cope with abiotic stress or microbial infection, as well as for ROS production (Walters, 2003a ). Recent studies have also demonstrated that polyamines are crucial for bacterial pathogenicity (Shi et al., 2019 ) and fungal growth, development, and pathogenicity (Valdes‐Santiago, Cervantes‐Chavez, Leon‐Ramirez, et al., 2012 ). However, detailed information about the metabolism, biological functions, and regulatory mechanisms of polyamines (including PUT, SPD, and SPM) is still lacking in the sugarcane smut fungus S. scitamineum .

Sexual mating and the following filamentation are critical for virulence in dimorphic fungi, including U. maydis (Kahmann et al., 1995 ; Spellig et al., 1994 ), Candida albicans (Mitchell, 1998 ), Cryptococcus neoformans (Wickes et al., 1996 ), and also S. scitamineum (Chang et al., 2019 ; Yan, Zhu, et al., 2016 ; Zhu et al., 2019 ). In the present work, we demonstrated that PUT at high concentrations suppressed S. scitamineum sexual mating/filamentation (Figure 2b ). In contrast, SPD promoted filamentation (Figure 2b ). We further showed that SsAGA, SsODC, and SsSAMDC are involved in different steps of polyamine biosynthesis in S. scitamineum . It is known that AGA and ODC contribute to PUT production through the ornithine pathway; in parallel, the arginine pathway contributes to PUT production through sequential reactions catalysed by ADC, AIH, and AGT (Miller‐Fleming et al., 2015 ; Valdes‐Santiago, Cervantes‐Chavez, Leon‐Ramirez, et al., 2012 ). Our study showed that loss of SsODC and SsSAMDC caused auxotrophy for PUT and SPD (Figure 1a,b ), indicating that the ornithine pathway plays a predominant role in PUT biosynthesis in S. scitamineum . Sexual mating/filamentation were defective to various degrees in polyamine mutants, which differentially responded to exogenous addition of PUT or SPD (Figure 2a ). We infer that the intracellular levels of polyamines need to be maintained at a reasonable concentration, and excessive polyamines within a cell may be detrimental. Interestingly, SPM is absent in U. maydis (Valdes‐Santiago et al., 2009 ), but it was detectable in S. scitamineum in the present study. The importance of polyamines has been demonstrated in other phytopathogenic fungi, including the corn smut fungus U. maydis . The U. maydis spe and samdc mutants, which are defective in SPD biosynthesis, are compromised in dimorphic transition and hypersensitive towards different stress conditions (Guevara‐Olvera et al., 1997 ; Valdes‐Santiago, Cervantes‐Chavez, Winkler, et al., 2012 ). It has also been reported that the ODC gene of Stagonospora ( Septoria ) nodorum is required for virulence towards wheat (Bailey et al., 2000 ). For Fusarium species, SPD is essential for growth, development, production of the mycotoxin deoxynivalenol (DON), and virulence (Tang et al., 2021 ).

A striking increase in maize polyamine biosynthesis, mainly free and conjugated PUT, occurs in tumours induced by the fungus and in the neighbouring plant tissues during the interaction with the biotrophic pathogenic fungus U. maydis (Rodriguez‐Kessler et al., 2008 ; Rodriguez‐Kessler & Jimenez‐Bremont, 2009 ). A strong increase in ODC and ADC transcript levels and the consequent accumulation of PUT were detected following inoculation of Fusarium graminearum to host plants (Gardiner et al., 2010 ). Polyamine levels increase in smut teliospores after the perception of sugarcane glycoproteins (Sanchez‐Elordi et al., 2019 ). SPM plays an important role in the infection of rice leaves by Magnaporthe oryzae , probably through redox buffering in the endoplasmic reticulum (Rocha et al., 2020 ). Similarly, deletion of ChODC in Colletotrichum higginsianum results in defective hyphal and conidial development, significantly affecting appressorium‐mediated infection, which cannot be restored by addition of polyamines (Yan et al., 2022 ). These studies demonstrate that polyamines act as a virulence factor of phytopathogenic fungi. Similarly, our results proved that the fungal SsSAMDC and SsSPDS / SPMS genes were induced in the early stage of sugarcane infection, probably to promote SPD production to facilitate infection (Figure 3d ). Correspondingly, SPD accumulated in the diseased tissue (“whip”) and the proximal part of the stem below the whip (Figure 3e ). We infer that S. scitamineum may utilize SPD to promote filamentation and help colonizing the host cane. On the other hand, plants also utilize polyamines to regulate immunity against pathogens, notably by amplifying pattern‐triggered immunity responses through the production of ROS (Gerlin et al., 2021 ). PUT, SPD, and SPM are ubiquitous in plant cells, existing in free form, as cations covalently bound to proteins, or conjugated with hydroxycinnamic acid to form phenolic amides (HCAAs; Walters, 2003b ), which are a diverse group of specialized metabolites involved in plant resistance to biotic or abiotic stress (Fang et al., 2021 ). Therefore polyamines, either sourced from the fungus or the plant, may mediate interactions between pathogen and host, likely contributing to disease occurrence and/or severity.

The cAMP–PKA signalling pathway is essential for proper mating and filamentation, and thus critical for S. scitamineum virulence (Chang et al., 2019 ). In the present study, we showed that the SsODC gene was significantly up‐regulated in the ssgpa3 Δ, ssuac1 Δ, and ssadr1 Δ mutants (Figure 4b ), and exogenous addition of SPD or SPM could partially restore the sexual mating/filamentation defect in these mutants (Figure 4a ). We speculate that the sexual mating/filamentation defect in these mutants defective in the cAMP–PKA pathway is partially due to up‐regulation of the SsODC gene and the consequent elevated level of PUT, which was proved to suppress sexual mating/filamentation (Figure 2b ). Overall, these results indicate that the cAMP–PKA pathway regulates S. scitamineum sexual mating/filamentation by affecting polyamine biosynthesis. It has been reported that polyamines reduce intracellular cAMP levels in the rice blast fungus M. oryzae , leading to the inhibition of appressorium formation (Choi et al., 1998 ). In the present study, disrupted polyamine biosynthesis in the sssamdc Δ mutant did not cause any changes in the transcript levels of genes involved in the cAMP–PKA pathway. We found a direct interaction between SsGPA3 and SsODC (Figure 5a ), further supporting cross‐talk between the cAMP–PKA pathway and the polyamine biosynthesis pathway in S. scitamineum .

ROS are tightly associated with plant defence responses to bacterial and fungal pathogens. One of the initial defence reactions in plants after pathogen recognition is the ROS burst (Torres, 2010 ). Smut pathogens modulate ROS production and scavenging to affect defence responses in host plants (Peters et al., 2017 ). Polyamines play dual roles in maintaining cellular redox homeostasis by both protecting against free radical‐mediated damage and acting as substrates for enzymes that produce ROS (Murray Stewart et al., 2018 ). Based on the comparative transcriptome analysis of ss1aga Δ versus MAT‐1 and ss1aga Δ × ss2aga Δ versus MAT‐1 × MAT‐2 , we found that ROS marker genes encoding catalase ( CAT1 ) and glutathione S ‐transferase ( GST ) were both significantly down‐regulated in the ssaga Δ mutant (Dataset S2 ), which displayed significantly elevated intracellular ROS levels (Figure 6a ). This indicates a connection between polyamines and intracellular redox homeostasis. Besides, polyamine mutants were more sensitive to H 2 O 2 compared to WT ( MAT‐2 ) (Figure 6b ). We infer that PUT may cause accumulation of ROS while SPD has the opposite role. Supporting this hypothesis, addition of PUT led to down‐regulation of antioxidant enzyme genes, while SPD could promote up‐regulation of these genes (Figure 6c ). It has been reported that in Arabidopsis thaliana , PUT content is positively related to H 2 O 2 generation via activating the copper‐containing amine oxidase CuAO (Liu & Alcazar, 2021 ). Consistently, we found that the CuAO‐encoding gene AO1 ( SPSC_00335 ) was up‐regulated in ss1aga Δ compared to the WT MAT‐1 (Dataset S2 ), based on the comparative transcriptome analysis. We speculate that excessive PUT in ss1aga Δ can be oxidized by AO1 to produce H 2 O 2 , causing defective filamentation. On the other hand, it has been reported that SPD could reduce intracellular ROS levels and relieve endoplasmic reticulum stress in diabetic mouse hearts (Sun et al., 2023 ). Our finding that SPD suppresses intracellular ROS production by inducing expression of antioxidant enzyme genes is consistent with what has been reported in animal cells.

In summary, we elucidated the polyamine biosynthesis pathway, which is probably dependent on the ornithine pathway (SsAGA and SsODC) for PUT production and on SsSAMDC for PUT‐to‐SPD conversion, in S. scitamineum . Our study provides evidence that polyamine biosynthesis and the cAMP–PKA signalling pathway physically and genetically interact with each other, to promote sexual mating/filamentation by decreasing intracellular PUT levels while increasing SPD levels. Homeostasis of intracellular polyamines contributes to interaction between S. scitamineum and sugarcane, probably by modulating intracellular redox homeostasis. In the future, it is worth exploring the molecular mechanism of polyamines involved in phytopathogen–host interaction, particularly the direct target(s) of polyamines, in both fungi and plants.
